LLMs and Generative AI — Roadmap
A focused path for engineers who want to build with and on top of large language models.
Assumes you already know Python well. Realistic timeline: 4–6 months at 15+ hours/week to
become genuinely productive.
The ﬁeld moves fast, but the fundamentals don't. Spend ~30% of your time on durable
concepts, ~70% on building.
Prerequisites (skip if you have them)
Python — ﬂuent, including async, classes, type hints
Basic ML literacy — what training, inference, loss, and gradients mean. You don't need to
train models from scratch.
Linear algebra intuition — vectors, dot products, matrix multiplication. Conceptual is ﬁne.
HTTP, JSON, REST APIs — you'll be calling APIs constantly
Git and a basic Linux command line
If any of these are weak, ﬁx that ﬁrst. A week of remediation saves a month of confusion.
Phase 1 — How LLMs actually work (2–3 weeks)
You don't need to train a frontier model, but you should understand what's happening when you
call one. Surface-level intuition is the diﬀerence between someone who debugs prompts blindly
and someone who reasons about them.
Concepts to internalize:
Tokenization — why "strawberry" has weird spelling issues, why prices in tokens matter
Embeddings — vectors representing meaning, why similarity search works
The transformer architecture — attention, context windows, KV cache
Pretraining vs. post-training (instruction tuning, RLHF, DPO, RLAIF)
Sampling — temperature, top-p, top-k, why deterministic output isn't quite real
Context windows, positional encoding, the cost of long contexts
Reasoning models vs. standard models — what "thinking" tokens actually do
Best resources:
Andrej Karpathy's Let's build GPT and Let's build the GPT Tokenizer on YouTube — non-
negotiableJay Alammar's Illustrated Transformer and Illustrated GPT-2
3Blue1Brown's transformer / attention videos
Attention Is All You Need (read it once, even if uncomfortable)
Project: Build a tiny character-level transformer in PyTorch following Karpathy's nanoGPT.
Don't skip this — touching the math once makes everything else click.
Phase 2 — Working with LLM APIs (3–4 weeks)
This is where most real-world LLM engineering happens.
Get hands-on with multiple providers — Claude (Anthropic), GPT (OpenAI), Gemini (Google),
and at least one open model via Together / Groq / Fireworks / Ollama. Each has quirks. Don't lock
into one.
Core skills:
Prompt engineering — system prompts, few-shot examples, chain-of-thought, role
assignment
Structured output — JSON mode, schema-constrained generation, Pydantic with
instructor
Function calling / tool use
Streaming responses
Prompt caching, batching, and cost management
Handling rate limits, retries, and timeouts gracefully
Reasoning / extended-thinking modes — when to use them, how they cost more
Multi-turn conversation management
Token counting and context management
Patterns to learn:
Prompt chaining (output of one call feeds the next)
Routing (classiﬁer picks which prompt/model handles a query)
Self-critique and revision loops
Parallelization for independent subtasks
Best resources:
Anthropic's prompt engineering docs and Claude cookbook
OpenAI cookbook
Prompt Engineering Guide (promptingguide.ai)Hamel Husain's blog on LLM evaluation and engineering
Project: Build a CLI tool that does something genuinely useful for you — a code reviewer for your
own commits, a meeting-notes summarizer, a research assistant. Not a chatbot. Something you'll
actually use.
Phase 3 — Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) (4–6 weeks)
The most common production pattern. Easy to demo, hard to do well.
Foundations:
Embedding models — OpenAI, Cohere, Voyage, BGE, Nomic, Jina. Understand tradeoﬀs.
Vector databases — start with pgvector (Postgres) for real apps; learn Chroma for
prototyping; know Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus exist
Cosine similarity vs. dot product vs. Euclidean
ANN algorithms (HNSW) at a conceptual level
The unsexy parts that actually matter:
Chunking strategy — ﬁxed-size, semantic, recursive, document-structure-aware. This
makes or breaks retrieval quality.
Hybrid search — combining dense (embeddings) and sparse (BM25) retrieval
Reranking — Cohere Rerank, cross-encoders. Almost always improves results.
Query transformation — HyDE, query expansion, multi-query
Metadata ﬁltering — often more important than fancy embeddings
Citation and grounding — making the LLM cite sources reliably
Evaluation (critical):
Retrieval metrics: recall@k, MRR, NDCG
Generation metrics: faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision
Tools: Ragas, custom eval sets. Build your eval set before you optimize.
Project: RAG over a real corpus you care about — your notes, a textbook, company docs, a
podcast archive. Build the eval set ﬁrst. Iterate on retrieval until your numbers actually improve.
Phase 4 — Agents and tool use (4–6 weeks)
The frontier of applied LLM engineering. Also where most demos break in production.
Concepts:Tool/function calling — the foundation of all agents
ReAct pattern (reason → act → observe → loop)
Planning vs. reactive agents
Memory: short-term (context), long-term (vector store), episodic
Multi-agent systems — when they help, when they're overkill (often the latter)
Human-in-the-loop and approval gates
Speciﬁc topics worth learning:
MCP (Model Context Protocol) — the emerging standard for tool integration
Computer use / browser agents (Anthropic, OpenAI Operator-style)
Code execution as a tool (sandboxing, safety)
Cost and latency control for multi-step agents
Loop detection and termination
Frameworks (use sparingly):
LangGraph — stateful agent ﬂows, the most useful framework
LlamaIndex — strong for retrieval-heavy agents
Pydantic AI — clean, type-safe, growing fast
Plain Python and direct API calls — often the right answer; frameworks add complexity you
may not need
Anthropic's Building Eﬀective Agents post is the best practical guide on when to use what
pattern. Read it.
Project: Build an agent that does something genuinely multi-step and useful — a code-
modiﬁcation agent, a research agent that produces cited reports, a personal automation agent.
Make it robust to failure.
Phase 5 — Evaluation (do this throughout, not after)
This is the skill that separates LLM engineers from people who just glue prompts together. Most
teams underinvest here and pay for it.
Build eval sets early. Even 20 hand-curated examples beats no evals.
LLM-as-judge — when it works, when it lies. Pairwise comparisons usually beat absolute
scoring.
Reference-based vs. reference-free evaluation
Regression testing — run evals on every prompt changeProduction observability — Langfuse, LangSmith, Helicone, Braintrust, Arize
Online evals — sampling production traﬃc for human review
Hamel Husain's writing on evals is the canonical resource. Eugene Yan's blog is also excellent.
Phase 6 — Fine-tuning and post-training (3–4 weeks)
Don't ﬁne-tune until you've exhausted prompting and RAG. When you do need it:
PEFT methods — LoRA, QLoRA. Almost never do full ﬁne-tunes.
Hugging Face transformers, peft, trl, datasets
Instruction tuning vs. continued pretraining vs. preference optimization
DPO and its variants (KTO, ORPO, IPO) — the modern alternative to RLHF
Synthetic data generation for ﬁne-tuning datasets
Distillation — ﬁne-tuning small models on big-model outputs
Quantization for inference: GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF, FP8
When to ﬁne-tune:
Style/format you can't get reliably with prompting
Domain language a base model doesn't know
Cost/latency reduction by distilling a frontier model into a small one
Privacy requirements ruling out hosted APIs
Project: Fine-tune a small open model (Qwen, Llama, Mistral, Gemma in the 3–8B range) on a
focused task using LoRA. Compare to a well-prompted frontier model with proper evals.
Phase 7 — Production, inference, and deployment (3–4 weeks)
Inference servers: vLLM, TGI, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM. vLLM is the default starting point.
Local/edge: Ollama, llama.cpp, MLX (Apple Silicon)
Hosted inference: Together, Fireworks, Groq, Anthropic/OpenAI/Google, Bedrock, Vertex
Serving patterns: streaming, speculative decoding, preﬁx caching, batching
Cost engineering: prompt caching, model routing (cheap model ﬁrst, escalate on failure),
aggressive context trimming
Latency: time to ﬁrst token vs. total time, why streaming matters for UX
Safety: input ﬁltering, output moderation, prompt injection defense, jailbreak handling
Privacy: PII handling, data retention, on-prem vs. hosted decisions
